prize_parts.citation: For the conception and construction of the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I still hold B007 as my preferred prize, but on a narrower basis than in round 1. The cited achievement is the conception and construction of IceCube and the detection of a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos beyond 100 TeV, a measured result that opened a new observational window and addressed a question as old as cosmic-ray physics. The instrument and the discovery are one connected achievement, and I no longer let the citation lean on TXS 0506+056 or the Galactic plane, which colleagues rightly describe as still maturing. Nobody in the first round disputed that the diffuse flux is secure, and nobody argued that B007 is premature in the sense of an unreplicated result. The disagreement is about discovery character and about credit, not about the science. On discovery character my view is unchanged: a detector that creates a messenger that did not exist is the kind of discovery the prize was written for, while a gain in accuracy, however remarkable, is a gain of degree. I recognise that this is a judgement of weighting, not a fact, and that five colleagues weigh it differently.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real and I have not removed it. In a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA and Baikal as precursors and Yoshida omitted from a two-name credit, any choice is representative and not decisive, and four colleagues (Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig) said so independently. Most of the diffuse flux still has no identified source, so the astrophysical interpretation is incomplete. B018, by contrast, has five first-round supporters, the cleanest two-name attribution on the shortlist and no member who calls it premature. My field is adjacent to IceCube, so I should discount my own enthusiasm. If the committee judges that a clean attribution outweighs discovery character, B018 is a legitimate and defensible choice, and I would not regard it as a poor prize.

responses.point: Asks what settles the Karle and Yoshida question, since that decides whether B007 is a two-name or three-name prize, and says the source astronomy is not yet mature next to the 1e-18 clock record.
responses.response: I accept the second point in full and have rewritten my citation so that it rests on the diffuse flux alone. On the first, I cannot settle Karle against Yoshida from the supplied material, and I will not pretend to. My reason for Halzen and Karle is a choice of role, not a ranking of contribution: Halzen drove the concept and the science case through AMANDA to IceCube, and Karle was central to turning the design into a working cubic kilometre of ice, which is what the 2013 result depended on. Yoshida's analysis and institutional contributions are substantial, and a three-name version is defensible, but it dilutes the instrument story and adds a name to a list that could then be extended without a stopping rule. I concede that this leaves B007 with a more discretionary credit than B018, and that is the main reason I now call B018 a serious fallback and not a lesser one.

responses.point: Says that for a collaboration of hundreds any two or three names are a representative choice, that the chair's pair excludes Yoshida, and that fluctuation theorems have a cleaner paper-level attribution even though the instrument case is stronger.
responses.response: Your point about representative choices is correct, and I do not claim that Halzen and Karle are uniquely determined. I would put the test differently, though. The question is whether the achievement is attributable to a small number of people who conceived it and made it work, not whether every contributor can be named, and for a detector built over a decade I believe the answer is yes, with discretion. Your own concession that the instrument case is stronger matters to me, since you place paper-level cleanliness above it. On B002 I remain unconvinced for a different reason: with four names for three places and the choice among the steady-state relation, the work equality and trajectory-level entropy production still open, the credit is not cleaner in practice, it is only cleaner in the first paragraph. I have not moved to B002.

responses.point: Argues that the lattice-clock result is established regardless of the redefinition of the second, that the 2005 comb prize covers a different invention, and that attribution for B018 is unusually clear.
responses.response: You have moved me on the redefinition of the second: a scientific prize should not wait for a metrological calendar, and I withdraw that as a reason against B018. I also accept that Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is not contained in the comb. Where we still differ is on what a prize recognises. The clock refines a measurement we already knew how to make, to a spectacular degree, and I would want the committee to say openly that it prefers that, rather than reach it by counting first places. You and I agree on the clean attribution of B018 and on IceCube being the strongest alternative. My configuration has not changed, but I am now closer to your position on timing than I was.

responses.point: Says the IceCube attribution is weaker because of the collaboration and precursors, that sources of most of the flux are unidentified, and that she could support B007 if the committee puts a high premium on a discovery of nature.
responses.response: That is a fair summary and I take the offer in the spirit in which it was made. I accept that the unidentified sources limit the interpretation, which is why the citation now cites the flux and the detector only. On attribution I would add one point: the AMANDA predecessor was largely the same group, so Halzen and Karle carry continuity from the precursor into the cubic-kilometre instrument, which is a partial answer to the precursor objection but not to the collaboration-size objection. Your own caution about the priority sequence for the lattice clocks is also the right one, and I note that no member has verified it; that is an uncertainty for B018 that I weigh against it only lightly.

responses.point: Prefers the compact Cirac and Zoller theory pair over an experimental co-laureate, and separates the 2022 and 2025 quantum prizes from the architecture of gates and simulators.
responses.response: Your separation of the recent prizes from B032 persuades me that timing is not an obstacle, and I keep B032 as an alternative for that reason. My remaining concern is the one you and Eriksson both raise: B032 overlaps with B015, where Cirac and Zoller appear again, so a prize on one affects the other, and the experimental realisations with ions and atoms would be left largely to the earlier 2012 prize. A theory-only prize can be coherent, but it needs the committee to accept that the experimental pioneers will be recognised separately, if at all. I think that is a harder sell than B007, where the instrument and the discovery come in one package, but I would not oppose it.

uncertainties: Whether any two-name IceCube credit can be defended against the collaboration, AMANDA predecessors and Yoshida; I cannot resolve it from the supplied material.
Whether the committee weighs a new observational window above a measured precision advance; this is a judgement of weighting, and my own field proximity may bias it.
The sources of most of the diffuse flux remain unidentified, so the astrophysical interpretation is incomplete.

I rely on existing knowledge of the 2013 discovery and later milestones and have not verified significance figures or the priority sequence between early lattice-clock proposals and first operating clocks.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. My profile records PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite and XL-Calibur connections and an astroparticle background adjacent to IceCube, but no documented tie to Halzen, Karle or Yoshida, and no tie to the credited names of B018 or B032. I flag the field proximity as a possible source of bias, not as a recusal ground, and I ask colleagues to read my preference for B007 with that in mind.
